solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Plant feature close to lake bedded by contrary gardener

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is wanted
something bedded by another is tucked inside it, as in a bed

blocks.note: the chin is a facial feature
the last letter of lake
from the nursery rhyme 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary, how does your garden grow?'

explanation.surface: A gardener with a contrary streak has planted some feature right by the edge of a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks botanical beside the gardener, but it means industrial equipment. CHIN plus E is tucked into MARY, the contrary gardener of the nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: Plant in the industrial sense means the machines and equipment used in a factory or works.

clue.text: Great distance, around 100 kilometres

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it on both sides

blocks.note: a mile is a unit of distance
C is the Roman numeral for 100
K is the usual abbreviation for kilometres

explanation.surface: Someone describes a long journey as roughly a hundred kilometres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great distance' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'Great' and the distance is MILE, wrapped around C and K.
explanation.definitionFit: Mickle is an old Scots and northern English word meaning much or large, as in the proverb about many a mickle.

clue.text: Molière can upset formalities

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters get jumbled

blocks.note: the playwright's name with the word after it, used as letters

explanation.surface: The French comic playwright Molière was known for mocking and overturning social conventions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a verb joining the sentence, but its letters belong in the anagram with the playwright's name; the accent on the E is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, ceremonial means the prescribed rites and protocol of an occasion, the set of formalities to be observed.

clue.text: Example of batting position?

blocks.note: in cricket the side batting is said to be in
a stance is a body position, like a batter's at the crease

explanation.surface: A coaching manual shows an illustration of how a cricketer stands to bat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batting position' suggests a place in the batting order; instead 'batting' is IN, as a cricket side batting is in, and 'position' is STANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a single case or illustration of something, which is what an example is.

clue.text: Film featuring Germany’s extremists and power in the country

indicators.note: to feature something is to include it, so one piece appears within another
extremes of a word are its outermost ends, so first and last letters

blocks.note: ET is Spielberg's film about the extra-terrestrial
the first and last letters of Germany
P is the symbol for power

explanation.surface: A film about German political extremists and their grip on power across the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremists' reads as political radicals, but it asks for the extreme letters of Germany, G and Y; those and P go inside ET.
explanation.definitionFit: Egypt is a North African nation, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: Measure credit extended to Met office?

blocks.note: Scotland Yard is the Metropolitan Police headquarters, so the Met's office is the Yard; with the possessive, YARD'S
buying on tick is buying on credit

explanation.surface: Someone asks how the Meteorological Office should be judged when given a line of credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Met office' suggests the weather forecasters, but it is the Metropolitan Police's base, Scotland Yard. Credit extended to it is the Yard's tick, and TICK is British slang for credit.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardstick is a standard used for judging or comparing things, so it is a measure.

clue.text: Talk idly about regular letters in biggest puzzle

indicators.note: letters at regular intervals means taking every second one
to be about something is to go round it

blocks.note: to jaw is to chatter at length
the second, fourth and sixth letters of biggest

explanation.surface: People chat aimlessly about the largest puzzle they have ever tackled.
explanation.walkthrough: JAW goes round the even letters of 'biggest'.
explanation.definitionFit: A jigsaw is a picture cut into interlocking pieces to be fitted back together, a kind of puzzle.

clue.text: Manage to wheedle some fizzy drinks, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is the spoken sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: Cokes are cola drinks, and the plural is pronounced the same as the answer

explanation.surface: Someone sweet-talks their way into getting a few sodas.
explanation.walkthrough: The drinks are Cokes; spoken, the plural matches the answer exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: To coax is to persuade someone gently by flattery or patience, succeeding through wheedling.

clue.text: Began meal, entertaining ace journalist

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in as a host does

blocks.note: lunch is a midday meal
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A dinner started by hosting a star reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entertaining' fits a host feeding a guest, and here the meal literally holds the ace inside it before the journalist is added.
explanation.definitionFit: To launch a project or campaign is to set it going, so launched means started.

clue.text: Proprietor of Venice bar sounded rough — in a state!

indicators.note: spoken in a rough accent, so we go by how it is pronounced with the dropped aitch

blocks.note: Harry's Bar is a famous Venice bar, so its proprietor is Harry's owner, said Cockney-style without the H

explanation.surface: The owner of a famous Venetian bar spoke hoarsely while drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry's Bar in Venice, home of the Bellini, is owned by Harry's owner; dropping the H, as a rough accent does, gives the sound of the answer. 'In a state' looks like drunkenness but hides the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Arizona is one of the United States, in the American southwest, so it is a state.

clue.text: Bob gets caught by Faye’s truck when reversing

indicators.note: something caught by a phrase is held within its letters
reversing means running backwards, so the letters read right to left

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A man called Bob is hit by Faye's lorry as she backs it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name but is a verb, a quick bending of the knees.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is a short bending of the knees in respect, which is what a curtsey is.

clue.text: East German boy receiving a kiss

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in

blocks.note: a son is a boy
taken as written
X stands for a kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A young lad from East Germany gets kissed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'East German boy' as one person, but the boy is just SON, receiving A and X.
explanation.definitionFit: Saxony is a state in eastern Germany, so a Saxon is a native of that part of the country.

clue.text: Excoriates MBAs Tesla sacked

indicators.note: a city that is sacked is ransacked and wrecked, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the business degrees and the carmaker, as letters

explanation.surface: A headline: business-school graduates fired by Tesla are tearing into the company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacked' fits the surface of fired staff, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To excoriate someone is to criticise them severely, and to lambaste is to berate or attack harshly in words.

clue.text: Way past locks that POW got around?

indicators.note: to get around is to move about, so the letters are moved into a new order

blocks.note: the word and the abbreviation for prisoner of war, as letters

explanation.surface: An escaping prisoner of war got past the locks on the doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' belongs to the jailbreak in the surface but means canal locks in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A towpath runs beside a canal or river, where horses once hauled barges, so it passes alongside the canal's lock gates.

clue.text: Disciple uncovered Mafia don — ciao! — shot

indicators.note: uncovered means stripped of its outer covering, so the end letters go
something shot is ruined and broken, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: the word without its first and last letters
the two words, as letters

explanation.surface: A gangland follower exposes the Mafia boss, who says goodbye and is gunned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' and 'shot' paint a mob killing, but the don is just three letters to scramble with the farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: An aficionado is a devoted enthusiast of something, much as a disciple is a keen follower.

clue.text: Vehicle securing parking, current Ford model

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast within

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
P is the sign for parking
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A car advert boasts of secure parking for this year's Ford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like 'latest', but it is the physics symbol I.
explanation.definitionFit: The Capri was a sporty coupé made by Ford from the late 1960s, one of the company's car models.

clue.text: Support journal covers novel format

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing covering another sits on top of it, so it comes first

blocks.note: a paper is a newspaper or journal
to back someone is to support them

explanation.surface: A magazine article backs a new way of publishing fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' could be an adjective meaning new, but it is the noun: a book of fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: A paperback is a book bound in flexible card covers, a common edition style for fiction.

clue.text: Appreciate timeless hotel inside Pune’s walls

indicators.note: less means without, so the letter standing for time is removed
walls are the outer boundary, so only the outside letters are kept
inside means placed within another

blocks.note: the Ritz, a famous London hotel, with its T for time dropped
the first and last letters of Pune

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys an ageless grand hotel within the old city walls of Pune in India.
explanation.walkthrough: The hotel is the Ritz; take out T and put what is left between P and E.
explanation.definitionFit: To prize something is to value it highly, which is to appreciate it.

clue.text: Dog restrained by lead beginning to sniff book

indicators.note: something restrained is held in check, enclosed by its restraint
the beginning of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
Rover is a stock name for a dog
the first letter of sniff

explanation.surface: A dog held back on its lead begins sniffing at a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' suggests a dog's leash, but it is the metal, symbol Pb.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbs is a book of the Old Testament, a collection of wise sayings.

clue.text: Struggle putting name in frame

indicators.note: putting one thing in another places it inside

blocks.note: a grid is a framework of crossing bars
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Someone battles to get their name onto a picture frame.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes into GRID.
explanation.definitionFit: A grind is hard, tedious and exhausting work, so it is a struggle.

clue.text: Girls getting upset with men — they’re such troublemakers!

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and thrown into disarray, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that girls get cross with men, who are always causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation reads as a gripe about men, but the definition covers the whole final phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Gremlins are imaginary mischievous sprites blamed for unexplained mechanical faults, so they cause trouble.

clue.text: Idiot losing pounds — an indefinite number — in card game

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it

blocks.note: plonker is British slang for a fool
L is the symbol for pounds sterling
N stands for an unspecified number in maths

explanation.surface: A fool loses an uncounted amount of money playing cards.
explanation.walkthrough: PLONKER is British slang for an idiot; take away L and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Poker is a gambling game played with cards, so it is an example of a card game.

clue.text: Evasive former pupil runs out of booze after leaving university

indicators.note: to be out of something is to have none left, so it is taken away
once something has left, it is no longer present

blocks.note: OB stands for old boy, a former pupil of a school
a liqueur is a sweet alcoholic drink
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: An old student, having left college, dodges questions when the drink runs dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs out of' looks like a phrasal verb about the drink running dry; actually R and one U leave LIQUEUR.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblique answer is indirect and roundabout, avoiding the point, which is what evasive means.

clue.text: Eccentric derivatives geek embracing India

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap arms around, holding something inside

blocks.note: a quant is a quantitative analyst, a maths specialist in finance such as derivatives trading
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An odd financial whizz-kid is mad about India.
explanation.walkthrough: A quant is a City numbers expert who models complex financial instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Quaint means attractively unusual or old-fashioned, which overlaps with eccentric in the sense of odd.

clue.text: Nocturnal horseman always features in teaching of Scripture

indicators.note: to feature in something is to appear within it

blocks.note: RE is religious education, the school subject
ever means always

explanation.surface: A ghostly night rider is a perennial figure in Bible lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nocturnal horseman' sounds like a ghost, but it is the American patriot. Religious education is the British school subject in which Scripture is taught.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Revere made his famous midnight ride in 1775 to warn colonists that British troops were coming.

clue.text: Recall my stroll gathering old aromatic plant

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters run backwards
to gather is to collect something in

blocks.note: cor! is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
an amble is a leisurely walk
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone remembers a walk where they picked an old-fashioned fragrant herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recall my' sounds like reminiscing, but 'my' is an exclamation, the British COR, which then runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Rocambole is a European plant related to garlic, grown for its pungent bulbs and used as a flavouring.

clue.text: Bud kicking Mike out of RV

indicators.note: kicking someone out ejects them, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: an RV, recreational vehicle, is a camper van
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A friend, a buddy, throws a man named Mike out of a motorhome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bud' looks like a pal, but it is a flower bud.
explanation.definitionFit: Capers are the pickled flower buds of a Mediterranean shrub, used as a sharp seasoning.

clue.text: Additional time to collect Times and Time?

indicators.note: collecting things means gathering them inside

blocks.note: an era is a period of time
x is the multiplication sign, read as 'times'
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone wants more time to fetch copies of The Times and Time magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Additional time' looks like a single phrase for extra time in football; only 'Additional' defines, and 'time' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means more than is usual or expected, added on, which is what additional means.

clue.text: Designate old hot bath no longer hot

indicators.note: something no longer present has been taken away

blocks.note: therm is an archaic word for a hot bath, from the Greek for heat
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: An old bathtub has gone cold and needs a name.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic word for a hot bath survives in thermal; remove the H.
explanation.definitionFit: To term something is to call it by a particular name, which is to designate it.

clue.text: Chatter involving defrocked Lima bishop?

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in as part of the whole
a defrocked priest is stripped of his robes, so the outer letters are removed

blocks.note: to prate is to talk foolishly at length
the word without its outer letters

explanation.surface: Gossip about a bishop in Lima who has been thrown out of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Defrocked' suits a disgraced cleric but strips Lima of its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A primate is the chief archbishop of a province or country, so a senior bishop; the question mark flags this as an example.

clue.text: Darkly brooding writer bored by year working

indicators.note: something bored is drilled through, with the borer then lying inside

blocks.note: a Bic is a ballpoint pen, a writing tool
YR is the abbreviation for year
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A gloomy author grows weary after a year of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' suggests an author, especially beside a brooding mood, but it is the pen brand, drilled into by YR and ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Byronic describes the moody, passionate, melancholy hero type associated with the poet Lord Byron.

clue.text: Reportedly checks shade that constrains pavement artist?

indicators.note: a report is something said, so we go by how the word is spoken

blocks.note: to curb is to check or restrain; the British spelling for the pavement edge sounds the same
a tone is a shade of colour

explanation.surface: A street chalk artist is confined to a strip of pavement edged by a dark-coloured border.
explanation.walkthrough: Kerb is the British spelling of the edge of the pavement, pronounced like curb.
explanation.definitionFit: A kerbstone is one of the blocks forming the pavement's edge, marking the limit of the area a pavement artist can use.
